title: Eight western states: a GeoClick pilot
intro: Let's learn eight western states with GeoClick. We're in Known mode: clicking a state reveals its name and a fact card.
We'll follow the Pacific coast south, then turn inland. The names we choose stay on the map, building a picture as we go.

states.name: Washington
lines: Start in the northwest corner: Washington. It's north of Oregon, with Canada above it and the Pacific coast to the west.
Its card explains that this is the only state named for a U.S. president: George Washington. Columbia was considered as an alternative name.
Remember Washington State here on the Pacific, far from Washington, D.C., on the other side of the country.

states.name: Oregon
lines: Directly south is Oregon, the middle state of our three-state Pacific coast chain. Washington above; California below.
The card says Oregon's name has an uncertain origin. Its other fact is firmer: Crater Lake is the deepest lake in the United States.
That lake fills a volcanic caldera. Pair Oregon with a deep blue lake inside a collapsed volcano.

states.name: California
lines: Continue south to California, the long Pacific state. Notice its angled eastern border: Nevada lies beyond much of that edge.
Here's the card's surprising name story: California was a fictional island in a Spanish adventure story, ruled by Queen Calafia.
So our coast chain is Washington, Oregon, California. Say those three north to south before we leave the ocean.

states.name: Nevada
lines: Now step inland to Nevada, east of California and south of Oregon. Its long sloping western edge fits against California.
The name means snow-covered in Spanish, referring to the Sierra Nevada. Think snowy mountains when you see the name Nevada.
The card also notes that most of Nevada's land belongs to the federal government. For our map memory, keep Nevada just inland from California.

states.name: Arizona
lines: Head southeast to Arizona. It's east of southern California, south of Utah, and touches Mexico along its southern border.
Its fact card introduces the Grand Canyon. Measured along the Colorado River, the canyon stretches about 446 kilometres, or 277 miles.
Use the canyon as your memory hook for Arizona. Next, we'll move straight north into Utah.

states.name: Utah
lines: Utah sits directly north of Arizona and east of Nevada. Notice the notch in its northeast corner.
The card connects Utah's name with the Ute people. It also points to the Great Salt Lake, the largest natural lake west of the Mississippi.
Remember this vertical pair: Utah above Arizona. Nevada is to Utah's west; Colorado is to its east.

states.name: Colorado
lines: Move east to Colorado, the broad rectangle beside Utah. New Mexico is directly below it.
The card gives us a striking elevation fact: Colorado's lowest point is higher than the highest point in eighteen other states.
That's a useful way to remember Colorado's high country. Keep Colorado east of Utah, above New Mexico.

states.name: New Mexico
lines: Our eighth state is New Mexico, directly south of Colorado and east of Arizona. Look for the small step in its southwestern outline.
Its card takes us to Trinity: the world's first atomic bomb test happened in New Mexico on July 16th, 1945.
Finish with two pairs: Utah above Arizona, and Colorado above New Mexico. Those four states meet at the point called Four Corners.

recap: Eight states, now visible together. Along the Pacific, north to south: Washington, Oregon, California. Inland from California: Nevada.
Then two north-south pairs: Utah and Arizona; Colorado and New Mexico. Pause here and trace that route yourself.
That's our eight-state pilot. We've explored their locations and facts in Known mode. A quiz can test what we remember next time.
